tagline: Four waterways connect lake ports, lighthouses and a trail that grew westward.
intro: The Great Lakes Seaway Trail links roads beside Lake Erie, the Niagara River, Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence River. The drive moves through cities, villages, bays and rolling farmland; in Pennsylvania, PA 5 parallels Lake Erie within 2,000 feet of the water at Lake City. The Federal Highway Administration lists the National Scenic Byway at 518 miles, recommends several days and highlights Niagara Falls, the Thousand Islands, lighthouses and War of 1812 sites.

William E. Tyson of the St. Lawrence-Eastern Ontario Commission conceived the trail in 1978. The original 80-mile route connected the Thousand Islands and Seaway International bridges. Extensions reached Niagara Falls in 1984, the Pennsylvania line in 1986 and Pennsylvania itself in 1996. National Scenic Byway recognition came to New York’s section in 1996 and Pennsylvania’s in 2005.

Traveling west to east, begin on US 20 at the Ohio line before joining PA 5 toward Erie. Continue along Lake Erie through Dunkirk and Buffalo, then follow the Niagara River toward the falls and Lewiston. Lake Ontario carries the journey east through Rochester and Oswego toward Sackets Harbor. At Cape Vincent, turn along the St. Lawrence through the Thousand Islands, continuing past Massena to the Seaway International Bridge.

moments.title: Presque Isle
moments.text: Presque Isle curves into Lake Erie, enclosing the bay that shelters Erie’s harbor. During the War of 1812, Oliver Hazard Perry used the bay to build six of his fleet’s nine ships. The peninsula forced potential attackers to sail around it to reach the shipbuilders. Wind and waves continue reshaping its sand, while breakwaters and imported sand help counter erosion. The Presque Isle Light, first lit in July 1873, has a red-brick former keeper’s house. The park’s first paved road arrived in 1924; Peninsula Drive now provides the main road approach, with 13 miles of roads within the park.
moments.notice: The Presque Isle Light has a red-brick former lighthouse keeper’s residence.

moments.title: Lewiston
moments.text: Niagara Falls began at the escarpment between Lewiston and Queenston, downstream of the present falls. Over roughly 12,500 years, erosion moved the falls nearly seven miles south, leaving the Niagara Gorge. The escarpment also shaped transport: in 1764, British military engineer John Montresor built an inclined wooden tramway here. Loaded carts climbed wooden rails, pulled by rope, to move goods over the escarpment. The tramway was known as The Cradles and the Old Lewiston Incline, names for the rope-and-rail system that carried loads up the slope. The village lies on the Niagara River across from Canada, between Niagara Falls and Fort Niagara.

moments.title: Sackets Harbor
moments.text: Warship building transformed Sackets Harbor during the War of 1812. The Navy established its Great Lakes headquarters and a major yard here, where more than 3,000 men worked. Soldiers built defenses and camped in the village; by fall 1814, the combined population ranked behind only New York City and Albany in the state. The war ended before the USS New Orleans was completed. Stored unfinished, it was finally scrapped in 1883. Navy Point now serves private boats as a marina. The village’s Main Street and preserved 19th-century buildings form the Sackets Harbor Village Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1983.
